## Chapter Outline

- Exploration and assessment of distant metastatic disease
- Mobilization and assessment of local resectability
- Resection phase
- Vascular resection
- Multivisceral resections
- Lymphadenectomy
- Reconstruction (pancreatic, biliary, GI continuity)
- Drains and nasogastric tubes

## Introduction: The Operation

- Pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) remains one of the few operations with:
  - Major morbidity rates ~**25%**
  - 90-day mortality of **2%–4%**
- Even at highest-volume centers with highest-volume surgeons
- Chapter describes approach to **exploration, resection, and reconstruction**

## Key Principles of the Chapter

- Multiple techniques shown to be equally effective
- Individual steps may — and should — be performed in different order depending on:
  - Nature of abnormality
  - Location of abnormality
- Emphasis on evidence-based decisions over opinion

## Open vs. Minimally Invasive PD

- Chapter focuses on **open PD** technique
- Minimally invasive approaches (laparoscopic and robotic) described in Chapter 127
- Developed over past 20 years
- **>95%** of these operations continue to be performed with open technique

## Minimally Invasive PD: Current Evidence

- Can be performed safely with equivalent outcomes to open approach
- Only in **very select high-volume centers**
- Requires a team dedicated to this endeavor

## Exploration: Assessment of Distant Metastatic Disease

- Initial goal: rule out **subradiographic metastatic disease**
- Metastatic disease = contraindication to resection
- Particularly important when operating for cancer
- Careful inspection of:
  - Liver
  - Peritoneal surfaces
- Targeted liver ultrasound for parenchymal abnormalities

## Staging Laparoscopy (SL)

- Use subject to individual surgeon preference and institutional experience
- Reported as performed:
  - Routinely
  - Selectively
  - Never
- Yield of SL **decreases** as quality of cross-sectional imaging increases
- Authors' approach: **selective, case-by-case basis**

## Indications for Staging Laparoscopy

- Concerning feature on preoperative imaging
- Significantly elevated **CA 19-9** level
- Degree of CA 19-9 elevation warranting SL varies:
  - Ranges from **130 to 250 U/mL** across studies

## CA 19-9: Important Caveat

- Attention must be paid to **status of biliary tree** at time of CA 19-9 evaluation
- Biliary obstruction can increase the CA 19-9 level
- Interpret elevation in clinical context

## Initial Incision

- When SL not necessary: begin with **limited upper midline incision**
- Initial incision small for:
  - Visual inspection
  - Manual inspection
- Rule out metastatic disease
- Once ruled out: extend incision to whatever length needed
- Safety of operation tailored to individual patient

## Mobilization: Wide Kocher Maneuver

- Performed to level of:
  - **Aorta**
  - **Left renal vein**
- Includes mobilization of **ligament of Treitz** from patient's right side
- Transverse mesocolon mobilized off:
  - Gerota's fascia
  - Head of pancreas

## Kocher Maneuver: Exposure Benefits

- Allows dynamic and manual retraction of:
  - Transverse colon
  - Its mesentery
- Retraction directed **caudally** to optimize exposure
- Enables assessment of:
  - Retroperitoneum
  - Relationship of mass with **superior mesenteric artery (SMA)**

## Kocher Maneuver: What to Avoid

- **No routine oncologic reason** to:
  - Enter Gerota's fascia of right kidney
  - Remove posterior aortocaval lymph nodes
- Both maneuvers may increase risks:
  - Lymphatic leak
- Provide **no proven oncologic benefit**

## Kocher Maneuver: Vascular Caution

- Avoid the **right gonadal vein** as it enters the IVC
- This vein is thin-walled
- If injured → **brisk bleeding**

## Artery-First Approach

- SMA inspected from ligament of Treitz
- Dissected on its right lateral surface
- Purpose: exclude tumor infiltration
- Helps with assessment of SMA involvement **early** in exploration

## Figure 117A.2: Artery-First Approach

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
- Superior mesenteric artery is dissected
- Infiltration of the artery is ruled out
- Performed as one of the **first steps** of the operation

::: {.column width="40%"}

## Authors' Practice on Artery-First

- **Do NOT routinely perform** this maneuver
- Rationale:
  - High-quality preoperative imaging typically adequate
  - Careful palpation in operating room typically adequate
- Both sufficient for excluding gross SMA involvement

## Access to the Lesser Sac

- Achieved through dissection of **greater omentum off transverse colon**
- Some surgeons enter lesser sac by directly dividing omentum near gastroepiploic vessels

## Why NOT Divide Omentum Directly

- May seem more direct and technically easier
- BUT results in **ischemic distal omentum**
- Branches from gastroepiploic arcade are divided
- In obese patients with significant omental bulk:
  - Ischemic tissue at risk for **postoperative infection**
  - Particularly in setting of postoperative pancreatic leak

## Advantage of Omental Preservation

- Healthy perfused omentum can be used as:
  - **Vascularized flap**
- Covers at conclusion of operation:
  - Pancreatic anastomosis
  - Biliary anastomosis
  - Gastroduodenal arterial (GDA) stump

## Identifying the SMV

- Dissection in avascular plane between:
  - Hepatic flexure
  - Duodenum
- Extension of Kocher maneuver separates third part of duodenum from colonic mesentery
- Avascular plane between gastroepiploic and middle colic veins divided
- Leads to **SMV at inferior edge of pancreas**

## SMV Dissection Details

- Several small crossing vascular branches may be encountered
- Should be **prospectively divided**
- Gastroepiploic vein may be ligated at this point
- Alternative: reserve until after pancreatic neck divided (more efficient)
- Early development of tunnel between:
  - Pancreatic neck
  - SMV and portal vein (PV) confluence

## Supraduodenal Compartment

- Retract stomach **anteriorly and inferiorly**
- Incise gastrohepatic ligament:
  - From lesser curve of stomach
  - To origin of right gastric artery (RGA)
- RGA retracted anteriorly
- Avascular tissue between GDA and RGA incised
- Expedites division of RGA

## Common Hepatic Artery Identification

- Reliably identified by removing lymph node anterior to it
- Known as **"common hepatic artery lymph node"**
- Also called **"the node of importance"**
- Involvement with disease may have prognostic value in pancreas cancer

## Node of Importance: Management

- Should generally be **removed** and sent for pathologic evaluation
- Should **NOT** be used as determinant of proceeding with resection

## GDA Ligation: Technique

- GDA encircled and **clamped**
- Ensure preserved pulse in:
  - Right hepatic artery
  - Left hepatic artery
- Excludes:
  - Misidentification of GDA
  - Tight celiac artery stenosis with hepatic inflow dependent on retrograde GDA flow
- Once deemed safe: GDA is **ligated and divided**

## GDA Ligation: Celiac Stenosis Scenario

- Must be prepared for **"what to do"** if pulse lost or diminished with clamping
- Careful preoperative assessment of high-quality contrast-enhanced imaging essential
- Clinically significant celiac stenosis evident on imaging through:
  - Arterial collateralization around pancreatic head
  - Enlarged GDA

## Managing Celiac Stenosis Intraoperatively

- Attempts to divide fibrotic attachments causing stenosis
- Rarely results in normal pulse (authors' experience)
- Even after clamping and division:
  - Intraoperative duplex ultrasound generally identifies continued flow in hepatic artery
  - In this setting: **proceed with resection**

## GDA Stump Blowout: Critical Concern

- GDA ligation **critically important** to minimizing morbidity and mortality
- GDA stump blowout:
  - Significant contributor to postoperative mortality
  - Reported in as many as **6% of patients**

## Protecting the GDA Stump

- Variety of tissue coverage techniques recommended:
  - Falciform ligament
  - Omentum
- Protect site of ligation from infection and leak
- Authors' technique:
  - **Triple ligation** (tie, suture ligation, clip)
  - Attempt to place omentum over stump at end of case

## Portal Vein Dissection

- Ligation of GDA exposes anterior surface of PV
- Anterior surface of PV dissected free
- Lateral border identified
- Lateral portal lymph nodes mobilized:
  - Away from bile duct
  - Brought down toward duodenum
  - Included in specimen

## Replaced/Accessory Right Hepatic Artery

- Present in **10%–15%** of patients
- Courses just **posterior and lateral** to bile duct
- Must assess for this
- Generally **preserved** if present

## When to Ligate Accessory/Replaced RHA

- In **absence of jaundice**:
  - Either accessory or replaced right hepatic artery can typically be safely ligated and resected if oncologically indicated
- In **setting of jaundice**:
  - Avoid ligation
  - Risk of postoperative **right liver necrosis**

## Final Assessment of Resectability

- Final assessment of:
  - Pancreatic neck
  - Overall resectability
- Many surgeons create tunnel behind pancreatic neck
- Ensures vein uninvolved OR safe resection possible if involved

## Authors' Approach to the Tunnel

- Attempt tunnel creation when vein does **not** appear involved on preoperative imaging
- When PV resection definitely/possibly required:
  - May not be safe to complete tunnel without some division of pancreas

## Decision Making with Vascular Involvement

- Determine whether reconstruction can be safely performed without complete tunnel
- Assessment of pancreatic neck and PV:
  - Critical
  - Can be subtly difficult
- **Intraoperative consultation with senior partners** should be considered
- "Good decisions come from experience, and experience comes from making bad decisions"

## Resection: Cholecystectomy

- Performed once deemed resectable
- Usually **anterograde fundus-down** technique
- In preoperative biliary obstruction:
  - Gallbladder can be distended and inflamed
  - Emptying gallbladder can facilitate dissection
- Cystic artery and duct identified and ligated

## Cholecystectomy: Vascular Caution

- Avoid iatrogenic injury to **right hepatic artery**
- Usually runs **posterior to common hepatic duct**

## Bile Duct Division Strategy

- Two approaches exist:
  - Leave gallbladder attached and divide common hepatic duct
  - Ligate cystic duct and later divide common bile duct

## Bile Duct Strategy by Disease

- **Pancreatic cancer:**
  - Positive bile duct margin generally not an issue
  - Ligate cystic duct, later divide bile duct
- **Cholangiocarcinoma of distal bile duct:**
  - Leave gallbladder attached
  - Later divide common hepatic duct
  - Goal: achieve **negative margin**

## Stomach Transection

- Transected with **two fires of GIA stapler**
- Just distal to the **incisura**
- Question of pylorus preservation has generated:
  - More than **8 clinical trials**
  - Over **three decades**
  - Over **1000 patients** prospectively evaluated

## Pylorus Preservation: Evidence

- Studies demonstrated **no difference in outcome**
- Debate over advantage/disadvantage is:
  - An exercise of **opinion**
  - Rather than exercise in **evidence-based medicine**

## Pylorus-Preserving Technique

- If preservation planned:
  - Right gastric artery divided **2 cm beyond pylorus**
  - Right gastroepiploic artery divided 2 cm beyond pylorus
  - Duodenum skeletonized
  - Duodenum divided
- Stomach along with omentum packed away in left upper quadrant

## Jejunal Transection

- Attention directed toward dividing:
  - Remaining ligament of Treitz
  - Jejunum
- Body wall retractors adjusted to expose ligament of Treitz
- Location of transection affected by:
  - Planned route of biliary-pancreatic limb
  - Via ligament of Treitz OR through transverse mesocolon

## Jejunal Transection: Key Principle

- Site of transection should allow:
  - **Ample mesenteric mobility**
  - **Tension-free anastomosis** for biliary and pancreatic reconstruction

## Jejunal Mesentery Division

- Mesentery divided close to bowel on specimen side
- Down to level of:
  - Root of mesentery
  - Uncinate process of pancreas
- Potential for postoperative hemorrhage from proximal jejunal mesentery
- Authors' practice: control vessels with **LigaSure device + clips**

## Ischemic Jejunal Limb

- Rotated **under the ligament of Treitz**
- Directed to **right upper quadrant**

## Pancreatic Neck Transection: Preparation

- Tunnel over PV fully developed
- Penrose drain or vessel loop placed into tunnel to encircle neck when possible
- Alternative: renal pedicle clamp to guide transection

## Pancreatic Neck Transection: Hemostatic Sutures

- Placed at superior and inferior borders of pancreas
- On each side of planned transection plane
- **Careful not to include pancreatic duct**
- Purposes:
  - Ligate superior and inferior pancreatic vessels
  - Decrease bleeding from cut surface

## Pancreatic Division Technique

- Superficial portions: divided with **electrocautery** (minimize bleeding)
- Deeper gland: divided **sharply with scalpel**
- Especially the pancreatic duct

## Bile Duct Division Timing

- Typically reserved for this point in operation
- Minimizes duration of bile drainage into right upper quadrant
- Especially important in preoperatively stented patients
- Some place clamp on distal bile duct to minimize bile spillage

## SMV-PV Dissection

- SMV-PV dissected away from pancreas and tumor
- Small venous branches controlled with:
  - Clips
  - Ties
  - Coagulation device

## SMA Dissection

- After vein completely freed
- Releasing posterior attachments of specimen to retroperitoneum
- Facilitates dissection along **right lateral plane of SMA**
- Specimen attachments isolated to lateral aspect of SMA
- Dissection completed along this plane to remove specimen

## SMA Dissection: Technique

- Specimen (pancreatic head, duodenum, proximal jejunum) retracted to patient's right
- Position of SMA **continuously assessed** to avoid injury
- Gentle retraction of SMV toward patient's left
- Anterolateral aspect of SMA completely skeletonized

## SMA Dissection: Instruments

- Small windows made in tissue
- Sealed with:
  - Ties
  - Clips
  - Coagulation device (e.g., LigaSure)
- Clips can combine with coagulation device
- Especially on **inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery**
- **Stapled transection should typically be avoided**
  - Particularly with concern regarding oncologic margin

## Venous Resection Strategy

- If venous resection required:
  - SMA dissection performed **first**
  - Venous resection left as **last step**
- Benefits:
  - Minimizes clamp time on PV
  - Allows more expeditious proximal and distal venous control

## Venous Control for Resection

- Control and often ligation of:
  - Inferior mesenteric vein
  - Splenic vein
  - Left gastric vein
- Necessary to isolate SMV-PV before venous resection

## After Specimen Removal

- Hemostasis ensured
- Operative field washed with **warm fluid**
- Proceed to reconstruction phase

## Vascular Resection: Historical Perspective

- More than 30 years ago: **Fortner** at Memorial Sloan Kettering
- Reasoned that more radical resection might improve survival
- Tumor adherence to PV/SMV previously criterion of unresectability
- Could be overcome by **en bloc resection** of involved vessels

## Vascular Resection: Authors' Approach

- When confirmed safe: reasonable to perform
- PV resection deemed appropriate in carefully selected patients
- Even **isolated hepatic arterial resection** appropriate in select patients
- **Routine SMA resection NOT considered appropriate**
  - 20% operative mortality
  - 11-month disease-specific survival

## Venous Resection: Systematic Review Data

- 52 manuscripts evaluated
- **6333 patients** with pancreatic resection for cancer
- **1646 patients (26%)** underwent synchronous portal/SMV resection
- Proportion of PV/SMV resections varied widely: **2% to 77%**

## Venous Resection: Operative Details

- Operations performed:
  - PD: **71%**
  - Total pancreatectomy: 24%
  - Subtotal pancreatectomy: 3%
  - Distal pancreatectomy: 2%
- Median operation time: **513 minutes** (range 168–1740)
- Median blood loss: **1750 mL** (range 300–26,000)
- Median PV occlusion time: **20 minutes** (range 7–302)

## Venous Resection: Outcomes

- Perioperative mortality: **5.9%** (range 0%–33%)
- Postoperative morbidity: **42%** (range 9%–78%)
- Venous invasion detected in **64%** of resection specimens
- Median survival: **13 months** (range 1–109)

## Venous Resection: Survival Rates

- 1-year overall survival: **50%**
- 3-year overall survival: **18%**
- 5-year overall survival: **8%**
- Based on 1351 patients undergoing PV/SMV resection

## Interpreting Pooled Data

- Substantially influenced by quality of each institutional report
- Standards of perioperative care, surgical technique, adjuvant therapy have improved dramatically
- Wide variations reflect heterogeneity in institutional experience

## Venous Resection: Modern Outcomes

- Long-term survival comparable to PD **without** vein resection
- As surgical expertise improves in high-volume centers:
  - Perioperative morbidity and mortality often similar to those without vein resection

## Venous Resection: Conclusion

- Venous involvement should **NOT** be contraindication to resection if:
  - Technically feasible
  - Acceptable morbidity/mortality at your institution
- Extent of resection individualized to:
  - Degree of tumor involvement
  - Patient's anatomy

## Borderline Resectable Disease

- Patients with venous involvement considered **borderline resectable**
- Should normally undergo some form of **preoperative therapy**

## Arterial Involvement: Contrast

- Poor prognostic factor for:
  - Short-term outcomes
  - Long-term outcomes
- SMA resection sometimes technically feasible
- **No data** suggest improved long-term survival
- Reported perioperative mortality is **high**

## PV Reconstruction Technique

- Depends on extent of involvement
- **Less than 1–2 cm**, not circumferential:
  - Interposition graft generally not necessary
- Adequate mobilization before venotomy important
- Defect almost always closed **horizontally**
  - Decreases narrowing of lumen

## Larger Venous Defects

- Interposition with:
  - **Autologous vein** (typically saphenous)
  - **Prosthetic**
- Historical concern over prosthetic:
  - Long-term patency
  - Tendency to infection (especially with pancreatic leak)

## Prosthetic Grafts: Recent Data

- Low risk for infection
- Similar long-term patency rates to autologous vein
- Approximately **75% at 1–2 years**
- Most surgeons consider aspirin or warfarin for patency
- **No data** support such approach

## Multivisceral Resections

- Utility addressed in several reports
- About **35%** of patients present with locally advanced pancreatic cancers
- Involvement of surrounding structures and organs
- Most often phenomenon of **body or tail** adenocarcinoma
  - Detected later
  - Larger size at diagnosis than head cancers

## Multivisceral Resection: Outcomes

- Extended resection morbidity historically increased
- Some reports show en bloc resection can be performed **safely** in well-selected patients
- No difference in:
  - Perioperative morbidity (35%)
  - Mortality (3%)
- Compared with standard resection

## Multivisceral Resection: Key Points

- Operative time longer
- Can include:
  - Mesocolon, colon
  - Adrenal glands
  - Liver
  - Stomach
- Blood loss and hospital stay NOT significantly different
- Primary goal: **R0 (margin negative) resection**
- Important predictor of long-term survival

## Lymphadenectomy: Rationale for Extended

- Positive lymph nodes confirmed outside confines of standard dissection
- Even for small cancers:
  - Para-aortic region nodes can harbor metastases
  - Between celiac trunk and inferior mesenteric artery
- Extended lymphadenectomy most popular in **Japan**
- Retrospective data: improved survival, similar morbidity/mortality

## Defining Extended Lymphadenectomy

- Consensus conference: **Castelfranco Veneto, Italy**
- Used Japanese Pancreas Society terminology
- Three types of lymphadenectomy during PD:
  - Standard
  - Radical
  - Extended radical
- For body/tail cancers:
  - Standard
  - Radical

## Extended Lymphadenectomy: Nonrandomized Studies

- Six prospective nonrandomized studies published
- Prospective study based on clinical status:
  - No significant differences in perioperative mortality
  - No differences in long-term survival
  - Trend toward better outcome in **standard** group
- Extended lymphadenectomy: increased rate of **severe diarrhea** early postoperatively

## Extended Lymphadenectomy: RCT Evidence I

- Four RCTs conducted
- Summarized in meta-analysis
- Studies from centers on **three different continents**
- Pedrazzoli study:
  - No differences in morbidity, mortality, survival
  - Retrospective subgroup analysis suggested benefit for node-positive patients
  - Validity of this finding debated

## Extended Lymphadenectomy: RCT Evidence II (Yeo)

- Largest study: **294 patients**
- Published 2002, updated 2005
- Randomized to standard vs. extended after negative frozen margins
- Heterogeneous tumor types
- Only **57%** pancreatic origin

## Yeo Study Results

- Perioperative mortality: similar between groups
- Long-term survival: similar between groups
- Morbidity significantly increased in extended group:
  - **43% vs. 29%** (P < .01)
- Much morbidity related to:
  - Delayed gastric emptying
  - Pancreatic fistula

## Extended Lymphadenectomy: Conclusions

- **NOT routinely indicated**
- Mayo Clinic and Japanese studies support same conclusions
- Increased morbidity without improved survival
- Reduction in quality of life:
  - Postoperative diarrhea
  - Subsequent malnutrition

## Current Standard

- For pancreatic head tumors:
  - **PD without extended lymphadenectomy**
- Except retrospective subgroup analysis (Pedrazzoli):
  - No RCT showed survival benefit
- Diarrhea and delayed gastric emptying more frequent with extended

## Reconstruction: Overview

- Three components:
  - Pancreaticojejunostomy
  - Bilioenteric anastomosis
  - Gastrointestinal continuity

## Pancreatic Leak: The Major Concern

- Major cause of **procedure-related death**
- Simply occluding pancreatic duct without anastomosis:
  - Higher fistula rates
  - Increased risk of exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
- **Drainage of pancreatic remnant to GI tract remains crucial**

## Pancreatoenteric Anastomosis: Principles

- Many techniques described
- Literature continues to report novel "safer" techniques
- Success most dependent on:
  - Surgeon's concentration
  - **Meticulous execution** of chosen technique

## Basic Tenets of Safe Anastomosis

- Careful handling of pancreatic tissues
- **Tension-free** adaptation
- **Good perfusion**
- **No distal obstruction**
- Any technique meeting these can have excellent outcomes

## PJ: Technique Options

- Most common structure: **jejunum**
- Two main approaches:
  - **Dunking procedure** (invaginating pancreas into end of jejunum)
  - **Duct-to-mucosa** technique
- End-to-side or end-to-end
- Technique does NOT significantly influence leak rate

## Pancreatogastrostomy (PG)

- Alternative organ: **stomach**
- Proponents cite:
  - Easier to perform (close proximity)
  - Less prone to ischemia (rich gastric perfusion)
- Original hypothesis: acidic environment prevents enzyme activation
  - **Not proven true**

## PJ vs. PG: RCT Data

- Prospective RCT comparison:
  - PJ leak rate: **11%**
  - PG leak rate: **12%**
  - Not significantly different
- Remember: trials typically randomize "institutional norm" vs. unfamiliar technique
- Institutional norm generally found superior or equivalent

## Authors' Preferred PJ Technique

- **Duct-to-mucosa PJ**
- **End-to-side** fashion
- **Retrocolic jejunal limb**
- Originally described by Editor Emeritus (LHB) of textbook

## PJ: Jejunal Limb Placement

- Jejunum brought to right upper quadrant via:
  - Ligament of Treitz, OR
  - Defect in mesocolon just right of middle colic vessels
- Authors prefer **latter** (mesocolic defect)
  - Less vulnerable to obstruction with local recurrence

## PJ: Preparing the Pancreatic Remnant

- Mobilized off splenic vein for ~**2 cm**
- Previously placed hemostatic sutures used to elevate gland
- Away from venous confluence

## PJ: First Layer (Blumgart)

- **Transpancreatic horizontal mattress sutures**
- Through and through pancreas
- ~1 cm proximal to cut transection edge
- **3.0 PDS** sutures
- Needle may be straightened for perpendicular path

## PJ: First Layer Details

- Start 1–2 cm from edge anteriorly
- Exit gland posteriorly same distance from transection edge
- Reconstruction started on **inferior edge** of gland
- Suture passed anterior to posterior

## PJ: Jejunal Suture Placement

- Seromuscular horizontal mattress suture through jejunal limb
- **Longitudinally oriented**
- Halfway between mesentery and anti-mesenteric bowel
- ~**3 cm** from stapled transected edge of jejunum

## PJ: Completing Horizontal Mattress

- Suture passed again through pancreas:
  - Entering posterior surface
  - Exiting anterior surface
- Keeping 1–2 cm from cut edge
- Creates horizontal mattress between full thickness of pancreas and biliopancreatic limb

## PJ: Number of Sutures

- Pancreas typically accommodates:
  - **2–3 stitches inferior** to pancreatic duct
  - **2–3 stitches superior** to pancreatic duct
- Probe placed in pancreatic duct to protect it
- **Needles left on each suture** for final anterior layer

## Figure 117A.5: Duct-to-Mucosa Preparation

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
- Corner and anterior row stitches placed in pancreatic duct
- Duct **tented open**
- Facilitates placement of posterior row
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
*[Figure showing duct sutures in place]*
:::
:::

## PJ: Duct-to-Mucosa Layer

- Pancreatic duct approximated to small full-thickness enterotomy in jejunum
- **4.0 PDS** sufficient for most cases
- 5.0 or 6.0 may be appropriate depending on duct size
- Enterotomy ~1 cm from line of horizontal sutures
- Allows tension-free adaptation

## PJ: Duct-to-Mucosa Sutures

- **4–6 sutures** fully approximate duct to jejunum:
  - Two at corners
  - One to two anteriorly
  - One to two posteriorly
- Helpful to place and tie **posterior suture first**
  - Better visualization of duct for remaining stitches

## Figure 117A.6: Anterior Row Completion

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
- After duct-to-mucosa layer complete
- Vicryl sutures tied down
- Inferior-most suture placed **vertically** in jejunum
- Second **horizontal bite** taken
- Jejunum folds over anterior surface of pancreas
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
*[Figure showing anterior layer technique]*
:::
:::

## PJ: Final Anterior Layer

- Previously placed 3.0 PDS sutures complete final anterior row
- Each suture tied down starting with inferior edge
- Imperative to **tie jejunum down to pancreas**
- Horizontal mattress sutures continued from inferior to superior edge

## PJ: Vertical Stitches

- Last stitch placed in **mirror image** to first inferior stitch
- Two bites in jejunum:
  - First vertical
  - Then horizontal mattress directed back toward pancreas
- Vertical stitches **wrap jejunum** around inferior and superior edge of pancreas

## Figure 117A.7: Completed Pancreaticojejunostomy

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
- **None of the duct-to-mucosa sutures should be visible** once anterior row complete
- Jejunum folded over anterior surface of pancreas
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}

## PJ: Technique Advantages

- End-to-side technique allows:
  - Adaptation of jejunal opening to specific requirements of pancreatic remnant
- Separate duct-to-mucosa adaptation:
  - Keeps duct orifice open
  - Ensures **unobstructed flow** of pancreatic secretions
- Authors **do NOT use pancreatic stents**

## Bilioenteric Anastomosis: Overview

- Less variability in construction
- Less likely to experience leak or fistula
- Can be fashioned:
  - Continuous technique
  - Interrupted technique
- Choice depends on size of bile duct
- Normally use **4.0 PDS** suture

## Bilioenteric: Continuous Technique

- Single-layer full-thickness anastomosis
- **Posterior layer completed first:**
  - Start at **3 o'clock** position
  - Stop at **9 o'clock** position
- **Second suture** completes anterior layer
- Prevents purse-stringing of anastomosis

## Figure 117A.8: Continuous Posterior Row

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

## Bilioenteric: Interrupted Technique

- Preferred for **small bile ducts < 5 mm**
- Anterior row and corner sutures placed first in bile duct
- Holds duct open for posterior row construction
- Small enterotomy in jejunum ~**6–8 cm** from PJ

## Figure 117A.9: Interrupted Technique

::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
- Completed posterior row
- Corner and anterior bile duct sutures in place
- Posterior row tied with **knots on inside** of anastomosis
:::

## Interrupted Technique: Anterior Row

- Anterior row and corner sutures passed through full-thickness jejunum
- Tied down starting with corner stitches
- Working toward **12 o'clock** position
- Knots tied **outside** of anastomosis

## Reconstitution of GI Continuity

- Classic PD: **antecolic gastrojejunostomy**
- Pylorus-preserving PD: **duodenojejunostomy**
- Concern about intact pylorus and DGE:
  - **Laid to rest** by several RCTs
- Based on 2004 evidence:
  - Pylorus preservation does **NOT** increase DGE frequency

## Delayed Gastric Emptying: Theories

- Retrocolic reconstruction may predispose to:
  - Venous congestion
  - Bowel edema
  - Slowed jejunal peristalsis recovery
- Postoperative gastroparesis:
  - Temporary gastric distension
  - Angulation of anastomosis in retrocolic position
- Close proximity of duodenojejunostomy to PJ:
  - DGE risk with PJ leak or remnant pancreatitis

## Authors' GI Reconstruction

- Regardless of classic vs. PPPD:
  - **Antecolic end-to-side** duodenojejunostomy or gastrojejunostomy
  - ~**50 cm downstream** from hepaticojejunostomy
- Transverse colon and omentum used to shield anastomosis away from PJ
- Single layer with **3.0 PDS** in continuous fashion

## Abdominal Drains: Historical Dogma

- Intraperitoneal drainage recommended for decades
- Intention: control leakage of biliary, lymphatic, or pancreatic secretions
- Prophylactic in nature
- Stems more from **surgical dogma** than level 1 evidence

## Drains: First RCT (MSKCC)

- Placement of drains did **NOT** reduce surgical morbidity
- Significantly higher proportion in drain group developed:
  - Intraperitoneal sepsis
  - Fluid collection
  - Fistula

## Drains: Heidelberg Trial

- 438 patients randomized
- No difference in:
  - Postoperative fistula
  - Fistula-related complications
- In-hospital mortality: **3% in both groups**

## Drains: Contrasting Data

- Multi-institutional study prematurely closed
- Higher morbidity and 90-day mortality in **no-drain** group
  - Mortality: **12% vs. 3%**
- Extremely high mortality not seen by others

## Authors' Drain Practice

- **Do NOT routinely place drains** after PD
- Based on two large RCTs showing no benefit
- Studies do not show clear harm with placement
- **Selective use** of drains is reasonable

## Early Drain Removal: Middle Ground

- Verona group prospective RCT:
  - Early drain removal by **postoperative day 3**
  - Associated with **decreased rates** of pancreatic fistula

## Postoperative Management Regardless of Drains

- **Early cross-sectional imaging**
- **Intervention** for evidence of undrained pancreatic collection
- Failure to rescue and mortality often attributed to:
  - **Late intervention** on early signs of sepsis

## Nasogastric Decompression: Evidence

- Meta-analysis refuted dogma of routine NG decompression
- Without NG tubes:
  - Fever significantly less common
  - Atelectasis less common
  - Pneumonia less common
  - Days to first oral intake significantly fewer

## NG Tube Considerations

- Abdominal distension or vomiting without NG tube:
  - Does NOT necessarily increase complications
  - Does NOT necessarily increase length of stay
- NG tubes omitted in most **enhanced recovery pathway** programs

## Authors' NG Practice

- Leave NG tube in place on night of surgery
- Remove on **morning of postoperative day 1**
- Trend toward omitting NG decompression in enhanced recovery protocols

## Summary: Historical Progress

- Surgical technique and outcomes advanced significantly since:
  - **Allan Whipple, 1935**
- Current expectations:
  - Operative mortality ~**1%** at high-volume centers
  - Median length of stay ~**7 days**

## Summary: No Single Advance

- No single advance, approach, or technique responsible
- Rather: **incremental and thoughtful investigation**
- By series of surgeon-researchers over decades

## Summary: Final Message

- Randomized data have **NOT** shown any single approach to be superior
- Every surgeon encouraged to:
  - Develop the approach that works best
  - For their patients
  - At their hospital

## Key Takeaways: Exploration

- Rule out metastatic disease first
- Selective staging laparoscopy based on imaging and CA 19-9
- Wide Kocher maneuver to assess SMA relationship
- Avoid routine Gerota's fascia entry and aortocaval node removal

## Key Takeaways: Resection

- GDA ligation: triple ligation, check hepatic pulse
- Beware celiac stenosis and replaced right hepatic artery
- Pancreatic neck: hemostatic sutures, sharp duct division
- SMA dissection: avoid stapled transection near margin

## Key Takeaways: Vascular Resection

- Venous involvement is NOT contraindication
- PV/SMV resection safe in experienced hands
- SMA resection: high mortality, no survival benefit
- Borderline resectable patients: consider preoperative therapy

## Key Takeaways: Lymphadenectomy

- Extended lymphadenectomy NOT routinely indicated
- Increased morbidity without survival benefit
- Standard lymphadenectomy remains current standard

## Key Takeaways: Reconstruction

- Meticulous technique more important than specific variant
- Tension-free, well-perfused, no distal obstruction
- Blumgart-style duct-to-mucosa PJ preferred by authors
- Bilioenteric anastomosis: continuous or interrupted based on duct size

## Key Takeaways: Postoperative

- No routine drains needed (selective use reasonable)
- Early drain removal if used (POD 3)
- No routine prolonged NG decompression
- Early imaging and intervention for collections
- Failure to rescue prevention is critical
